Nepal also warned of new flooding risks, with the country’s disaster authority saying water levels were rising in a lake formed by debris clogging a flooded site and that it was at risk of bursting its banks.
Rescue teams and military helicopters continue their search for hundreds of missing people along the mountainous border. Wednesday’s flash flooding after a glacial collapse killed at least 469 people and has left more than 1,500 missing.
Efforts to locate those unaccounted for have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 40km (25 miles) of roads. The missing include hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada.
The Red Cross said about 93,000 people might have been affected and launched an emergency appeal for $31m for disaster relief.
People rescued from an area cut off by flash flooding line up to register at an army camp in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Friday. Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP
China paused a rescue operation at the epicentre of the Tibet disaster due to the high risk of renewed flooding in Tibet. State broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by immense piles of debris had begun overflowing towards the area that rescue teams were headed.
Nepali army helicopter rescue teams are working to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project swamped by Wednesday’s flash flood, an army spokesperson said.
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said he ordered the release of $2m from the UN’s central emergency response fund to help with medical care, shelter and water.
Rescuers found bodies in Nepal’s Chitwan district, hundreds of kilometres downstream from the hardest-hit areas.
The overall death toll in Nepal has risen to 469 people, with more than 1,500 missing, and China has paused rescue work at the epicentre of the Tibet flooding amid fears that an artificial lake formed at the site was at risk of bursting.
The scale of the destruction from the flooding in Nepal’s northern border region was becoming clearer on Friday, with roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure destroyed and survivors describing scenes of extraordinary devastation.
Amid the rescue attempt unfolding at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
“There were at least 400 workers at the site,” Dev Shrestha, who was airlifted from the site where he was working, said after his rescue.
More people died than were rescued.
Worker Buddha Tamang said he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck – but he had managed to get out and reach help, Agence France-Presse reports.
“I survived as I was in the tunnel,” said Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours.
The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away.
Another worker, Arjun Kumar Tamang, spoke of “massive damage” at the hydropower site where he had been.
I don’t know how many people died but the force of the water swept everything away.
More now on the Nepali army’s rescue operation to save about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by Wednesday’s flooding.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.
The prime minister’s office said the army had been working in tough conditions.
“A Nepali army team has successfully rescued 350 workers and locals who were trapped in the tunnel a while ago facing extremely risky and challenging conditions amid adverse weather and rapid floodwaters,” the statement read.
The army is still working to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel.
Here are some of the latest images coming in amid the Nepal-Tibet border devastation as rescuers continue to search for more than 1,300 people missing, including hundreds of tourists and pilgrims.
A resident awaits news of missing relatives at a military camp in Trishuli, Nepal. Photograph: Ezra Acayan/Getty Images
Nepali army members prepare to leave on rescue missions in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Friday. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images
People move through a mud-covered road in Trishuli in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
Flash flood survivors receive medical treatment at an army base in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
A man looks at pictures of missing people at the Trauma Centre in Kathmandu, Nepal. Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters
Firefighters assemble near a drone during rescue operations after the mudslide in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China. Photograph: cnsphoto/Reuters
People (left) speak with the police as they search for their missing relatives at Bir hospital in Kathmandu. Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images
School children board a helicopter on a transit flight back to their family at Trishuli camp after being stranded by the flash flooding in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images
China halts rescue at Tibet epicentre over flood risk – state media
China has paused a rescue operation due to the high risk of renewed flooding in Tibet, where hundreds remain missing after the deadly mudslide in the border region.
State broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by immense piles of debris had begun overflowing towards the area that rescue teams were headed.
“So all rescue teams have been ordered to stand by in place and wait for further instructions,” it said on Friday, cited by AFP.
CCTV added that emergency teams which had earlier accessed the area “have been ordered to withdraw one kilometre”.
Rescue workers carrying relief supplies in Gyirong county in Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China, on Thursday. Photograph: China Daily/Reuters
Nepal army trying to rescue 100 trapped in hydropower tunnel
Nepali army helicopter rescue teams are working to rescue about 100 people trapped inside a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by Wednesday’s flash flood.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people ... some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Agence France-Presse.
The prime minister’s office said in a statement on Friday that 350 people had been rescued from the area but 100 more were trapped.
Nino Bucci and Henry Belot report that the mother’s sister Vaishnavi said she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.
They planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking as part of a tour.
Vaishnavi told the Guardian:
Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful. Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.
It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.
The 39 Australians missing in Nepal include Sydney family (from left) Shylaja, Aarush, Ashwin and Chandrasekaran Muralitharan; and couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan (bottom right) and Chitra Venkatraman (top right). Composite: Provided by the families
Nepal police have said that the death toll from Wednesday’s flash flood now stands at 469.
It’s a jump of 80 since the last reported update, and comes as search teams continue recovery efforts across the disaster-struck area. More than 1,300 remain missing, including hundreds of tourists from India, the US, Britain, Australia and Canada.
Efforts to locate those unaccounted for have been complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and 40km (25 miles) of roads in the mountainous region, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims.
Summary: river at risk of flooding again amid race to find survivors
Chinese authorities have warned that an artificial lake formed after a catastrophic flash flood hit the China-Nepal border on Wednesday faces a “high risk of breaching and sending flood waters downstream”, according to state media.
“According to forecasts, inflows into the lake could reach about 3 million cubic meters over the next three days amid continued rainfall, increasing the risk of a breach that could send flood waters downstream and potentially cause further damage in areas including Gyirong Port and elsewhere downstream”, state news agency Xinhua reported late on Thursday.
Nepal has also warned of new flooding risks, with the country’s disaster authority saying water levels were rising in a lake formed by debris clogging a flooded site and that it was at risk of bursting its banks. It did not name the specific site.
It comes as rescue teams and military helicopters continue their search for hundreds of missing people along the mountainous border, with the Red Cross saying about 93,000 people might have been affected. The aid agency launched an emergency appeal for $31m to respond to the disaster.
People walking in a flood-hit area in Nuwakot, Nepal, on Thursday. Photograph: Sulav Shrestha/Xinhua/AP
Also today:
Rescue teams and military helicopters are searching for hundreds of missing people along the mountainous Nepal-Tibet border after the huge torrent of water and mud swept through communities following a glacier collapse on Wednesday.
More than 390 people were killed, authorities in Nepal and China said, and more than 1,400 were missing, including hundreds of foreign citizens and pilgrims.
More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism officials said. Among those unaccounted for were 177 from India, 90 from the US, 39 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada.
Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said he ordered the release of $2m from the UN’s central emergency response fund to help with medical care, shelter and water.
US president Donald Trump said the flooding was terrible to see, describing how “strong, well-built buildings were wiped out like they were toothpicks”.
Nepaleseofficials said dozens of bridges were destroyed and nearly 40km of roads damaged, complicating search efforts.
The Nepalese army had rescued more than 100 people by helicopter, an army spokesperson said. Army teams also evacuated people trapped inside facilities linked to the Trishuli hydropower project, he said. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for medical care.
Rescuers found bodies in Nepal’s Chitwan district, hundreds of kilometres downstream from the hardest-hit areas.
The Nepal Red Cross Society said the agency has shifted its focus from rescue to large-scale relief operations in the flood-hit districts.
China’s premier, Li Qiang, arrived in Gyirong on Thursday to direct rescue efforts, alongside 500 military and paramilitary personnel.
This aerial image released on the Chinese social media platform Weibo shows a barrier lake which formed after a landslide near where Nepal's Chhochen Khola River flows into the Purepu Tsangpo River, in Gyirong county, in China's Tibet region.
Photograph: Lhasa Mobile Fire and Rescue Detachment/AFP/Getty Images
summary: The death toll from a catastrophic flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border has risen to 469, with more than 1,300 to 1,500 people still missing. Helicopter rescue operations were temporarily halted as authorities in both Nepal and China warned that debris-clogged artificial lakes were overflowing and at high risk of bursting. Meanwhile, the Nepali army successfully rescued hundreds of trapped individuals, including workers at a hydropower project tunnel, while international aid and emergency funds poured in.
key_points: The death toll has reached at least 469 people, with over 1,300 to 1,500 people remaining missing, including numerous international tourists.
Helicopter rescue operations were temporarily suspended after reports that dammed lakes formed by debris in the flood-hit regions began overflowing.
China paused its rescue operations at the Tibet epicentre due to the high risk of renewed flooding from an overflowing artificial lake.
The Nepali army successfully rescued hundreds of people, including workers trapped inside a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project.

Nepal's foreign ministry stated that the country does not currently require foreign assistance for search-and-rescue operations, though international aid organizations and nations have pledged humanitarian funds.

title: France to relax cheese production rules after drought takes toll on grazing land
author: Angelique Chrisafis
content:
Strict production rules will be loosened for some of France’s most famous cheeses after drought and repeated heatwaves dried out grazing pastures, threatening the livelihoods of traditional dairy workers.
Comté, a hard cheese made from raw cows’ milk in the Jura mountains, is France’s top-selling traditional cheese, with more than 62,000 tonnes produced last year. The government announced on Wednesday that its producers would be granted a temporary change to strict rules on grazing after farmers said extreme heat had scorched their pastures, putting production at risk.
Makers of beaufort and abondance, two cheeses made from cows grazed in the Alps, were also granted temporary changes to production rules because of the impact of the drought on grazing land.
All three cheeses carry the coveted label “appellation d’origine protégée” (AOP, protected designation of origin) to ensure their authenticity and protect traditional farming methods. This means producers must follow rigid rules on where their animals graze and what they eat.
![Brown cows graze in a lush, green mountain field with peaks in the background.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/6f7a52fe8780d9c221ccf08ae969e2be8e274641/0_0_4500_3000/master/4500.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
But the drought, which affected 95% of mainland France in July, has left normally rich green pastures dry, yellow and bare. French authorities said makers of comté, beaufort and abondance could temporarily supplement the animals’ diet with more fodder and grain brought in from elsewhere.
The National Institute of Origin and Quality (INAO), the government agency that administers and enforces rules on traditional food production, told Agence France-Presse it was also planning to grant temporary relief for the producers of several other cheeses including reblochon, cantal, bleu d’Auvergne, and fourme d’Ambert. It said the drought was “historic”.
Droughts are becoming more common and more severe in some parts of the world, including Europe, the fastest-warming continent, due to human-caused climate breakdown.
![A woman holds out a half-moon of artisan cheese with a thick, slightly mouldy rind and soft, creamy-looking pale yellow centre.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/629cb2e7e737ef1a31fe0cd4a64198e270efc009/0_0_7353_4912/master/7353.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
France’s numerous cheeses are a source of national pride and a key part of identity and local economy in rural areas.
Hubert Genty, a dairy farmer who produces neufchâtel cheese in Richemont in Normandy, said: “There really is no grass left to eat, this grass is totally scorched and has no value.” He told the TF1 TV channel his cows were producing less milk, which in turn would affect cheese production.
His wife, Angélique, who makes the heart-shaped cheeses by hand in the farm’s dairy, said she usually made 600 to 700 cheeses a day at this time of year and was now down to making 400-450 because of the low milk yield. She said she would struggle to meet customers’ demands.
![Large circular slabs of cantal cheese sit on a surface in a darkened cellar.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e447284455961c7b01b69e3606556f8434d39c9e/0_0_7360_4912/master/7360.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Farmers in many traditional French cheesemaking areas have warned about the damage of the drought and heatwaves. About 70% of producers of salers cheese, which has a protected AOP label, had to pause production over the summer because of the drought, the local newspaper La Montagne reported. Makers of roquefort have also called for a temporary easing on their traditional rules on grazing sheep, after many pastures were left scorched.
The French agriculture ministry’s statistical service said growth on permanent grasslands measured on 10 August was one-third less than the 1989-2018 average. The fodder situation was “highly degraded” in almost all regions, the ministry said earlier this month.
The agriculture minister, Annie Genevard, is expected to hold crisis talks with local authorities next week before announcing emergency measures for farmers.
![A half-moon of roquefort, showing its blue veins in a creamy centre. Its packaging bears a red stamp with the AOP designation.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/90ae68ebddf622e138fb381488af92feccb9f09d/0_0_5568_3712/master/5568.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Photograph: Bertrand Guay/AFP/Getty Images
The vegetable sector has been particularly affected. The French union of potato farmers, the UNPT, warned this week of a slump, saying it expected a “23% drop in this year’s crop “after five successive heatwaves and an exceptional lack of water”.
In the northern Hauts-de-France, a key potato-producing region, farmers said potatoes were much smaller than usual, raising concerns among local factories that produce chips, crisps and processed mashed potato.
Cider makers have voiced concerns about this year’s apple yield, and for many wine producers the grape harvest has begun early, amid uncertainty over the quantity of wine that will be produced.
summary: Severe droughts and heatwaves in France have scorched grazing pastures, prompting the government to temporarily relax strict production rules for famous AOP cheeses like comté, beaufort, and abondance. The historic lack of water has reduced milk yields and forced some farmers to pause production or supplement animal feed with grain brought in from elsewhere. Authorities are planning further relief for other traditional cheeses as the agricultural sector faces widespread impacts on dairy, potatoes, cider, and wine.
key_points: Producers of comté, beaufort, and abondance have been granted temporary rule changes to supplement dairy cows' diets with imported fodder and grain.
Strict AOP regulations normally require animals to graze on specific local pastures and follow rigid feeding guidelines.
The INAO plans to offer temporary relief for other cheeses, including reblochon, cantal, bleu d’Auvergne, and fourme d’Ambert.
About 70% of salers cheese producers had to pause production over the summer due to the drought.
Other agricultural sectors, including potatoes, cider apples, and wine grapes, are also experiencing reduced yields and early harvests.

title: Nepal flash flood: more than 350 killed amid warning of fresh danger from rising lake water – latest updates
author: Adam Fulton; Mabel Banfield-Nwachi; Martin Belam; Yu-chen Li; Nino Bucci
content:
A drone view shows mud covering buildings and property following devastating floods at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, on Thursday Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
A drone view shows mud covering buildings and property following devastating floods at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, on Thursday Photograph: Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters
New risk as lake in flood area threatens to burst as 353 confirmed dead
A lake formed at the site where the flood in Nepal occurred is rising and is at risk of bursting, the country’s disaster authority said, as it appealed to residents and rescuers to stay away from the river banks.
The blockage of a river on Wednesday led to the lake’s formation, Reuters reports the authority said.
Meanwhile Abi Narayan Kafle, the central spokesperson for the Nepal Police, has told AP 353 people were now confirmed dead in the floods as of Thursday.
My wife and I are heartbroken to hear of the devastating flooding that has struck the Nepal-China border.
Many in the United Kingdom have strong, deep and personal ties to this part of the world.
We send our most profound sympathy to all those who have so tragically lost their loved ones and we feel deeply for the many families awaiting anxiously the news of friends and relations.
Our hearts go out also to the families of all the police and Armed Forces personnel who lost their lives while carrying out their courageous duty in the service of others and we give our deepest thanks to those who have responded so selflessly in undertaking rescue efforts.
Our special thoughts and prayers remain with all those affected and, as always, the United Kingdom stands ready to help support those in need.
Kabita Dhungana, deputy mayor of Nuwakot in Nepal, the district affected by the floods, said “please help us”, as she spoke to BBC Radio 4’s The World at One about the flash floods her region is experiencing.
She said:
Family members, children, parents are missing, and this is a very critical bad situation…
Everything, basic needs are destroyed, so please help us. We are really in need of help.
Srijana Gurung, Plan International Nepal acting country director, said the climate crisis means floods and landslides are “far more frequent and intense”, as she highlighted the need of urgent medical care and risk of waterborne diseases in the aftermath of the floods in Nepal.
The statement said:
Across Nepal, communities are facing climate shock after shock with barely any time to recover. Floods and landslides have always happened in Nepal but the climate crisis is making them far more frequent and intense.
The priority now must be reaching those affected, supporting families searching for loved ones, and ensuring vulnerable communities have the assistance they need.
Children and their families who have lost their homes and livelihoods will be in urgent need of medical attention, shelter, water, food and hygiene kits. There is also a risk of waterborne disease as access to clean water and sanitation is likely to have been damaged.
Particular attention must be given to those most at risk, including girls, women, older people and people with disabilities, while ensuring their rights, safety, dignity and voices remain at the centre of the response.
New risk as lake in flood area threatens to burst as 353 confirmed dead
A lake formed at the site where the flood in Nepal occurred is rising and is at risk of bursting, the country’s disaster authority said, as it appealed to residents and rescuers to stay away from the river banks.
The blockage of a river on Wednesday led to the lake’s formation, Reuters reports the authority said.
Meanwhile Abi Narayan Kafle, the central spokesperson for the Nepal Police, has told AP 353 people were now confirmed dead in the floods as of Thursday.
Reuters has a quick snap that local media has reported that 332 bodies have now been recovered by authorities after the deadly flood in Nepal.
More than 900 people remain unaccounted for. In addition China’s state broadcaster has issued a figure of three confirmed deaths and more than 500 people missing in Tibet.
Rescue teams have found bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border.
Vivian Balakrishnan, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Singapore, said Singapore stands in solidarity with Nepal and China and pledged emergency assistance.
Singapore stands in solidarity with Nepal and China during this difficult time. We are putting together a humanitarian assistance package to support relief efforts in Nepal. A Consular Response Team will be deployed to assist affected Singaporeans on the ground.
Here are some of the latest images from the news wires.
More than 160 people have died and hundreds remain missing across northern Nepal after a suspected avalanche triggered massive flash floods and mudslides along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river near the Nepal-Tibet border. Houses in the Devighat Village, Nuwakot district, were among those affected. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA
Community stands together for thoughts and prayers for those affected by the disaster in Nepal. Diggers rest, Melbourne. Photograph: Jesse Thompson/AAP
An aerial view shows houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur Municipality, along the confluence of the Trishuli and Tadi rivers in Nepal's Nuwakot district. Photograph: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP/Getty Images
The IFRC (International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies), the world’s largest humanitarian network, posted a clip on X showing the destruction caused by the flooding.
It said Red Cross teams are on the ground with food, safe drinking water, emergency shelter materials, first aid and other essential supplies, though roads are damaged and access is “extremely limited”.
It wrote:
Severe flash floods have devastated northern Nepal, destroying homes, washing away bridges and cutting off communities.
Nepal Red Cross teams are responding with food, safe drinking water, emergency shelter materials, first aid and other essential supplies, despite damaged roads and extremely limited access.
The IFRC has released CHF 997,000 from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund, including an immediate CHF 100,000 advance to support urgent response efforts.
As the full scale of the disaster becomes clearer, we stand ready to provide further support and international assistance if needed.
Britain has pledged £5m and offered to send emergency responders to Nepal following the “devastating” flash floods there, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said.
Speaking to journalists during a visit to South Wales, the prime minister said:
It’s a devastating picture that is emerging from what has happened in Nepal.
Scenes that we’ve never seen the like before, I don’t think, certainly the scale of the devastation.
So there is immediate action being taken. We are deploying consular support staff to the region so that British nationals will be able to access support 24/7. An offer has been made of emergency responders to head to the region but that’s obviously a matter for the Nepalese government.
But also we’ve offered £5m to help with that response effort.
Obviously, there are a number of British nationals who currently are thought to be missing and we’ll be providing all the support we can to their families in what is a very distressing and devastating situation.
Nepal police say 270 bodies found after Himalayan flood
A total of 270 bodies have been found by authorities in Nepal after a torrential flood swept through the Himalayan border areas of the country and China’s Tibet, Reuters reports, citing what Nepal’s police said in a post on X.
Climate change is leading to conditions that can destabilise high-mountain rock and ice, strengthening prospects for disasters such as this week’s Himalayan flood along the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet, scientists say.
While the exact cause of Wednesday’s disaster is still being analysed, scientists say it probably began with a massive ice-rock avalanche on the northern slopes of Nepal’s Langtang Lirung peak into the Lhende Khola river on the Tibetan side.
Experts caution against describing climate change as the sole, immediate trigger for Wednesday’s collapse, though they say that rising temperatures and melting glaciers probably played a role in the disaster.
Simon Cox, chief scientist at the Mountains to Sea programme at Earth Sciences New Zealand, said:
Climate change is generating conditions that can destabilise high-mountain rock and ice.
That in turn makes collapses and cascading hazards of the kind seen this week more frequent, he added.
summary: Devastating flash floods and mudslides triggered near the Nepal-China border have resulted in hundreds of confirmed deaths and left many people missing. A newly formed lake at the disaster site is currently rising and threatens to burst, prompting disaster authorities to warn residents and rescuers to stay away from river banks. International organizations and foreign governments, including the United Kingdom and Singapore, are offering emergency assistance and humanitarian support.
key_points: Nepal police confirmed 353 deaths following the flash floods, while hundreds of people remain unaccounted for.
A lake formed by a river blockage is rising and poses an immediate risk of bursting, prompting warnings to stay away from river banks.
Scientists attribute the potential trigger to an ice-rock avalanche, noting that climate change makes such high-mountain disasters more frequent and intense.
International humanitarian networks like the IFRC, along with countries such as the UK and Singapore, are deploying relief supplies and financial aid.

title: Kremlin sources tell Bloomberg that Putin is preparing to escalate the war in Ukraine. A growing number of Russian officials believe that could eventually mean a tactical nuclear weapon. — Meduza
author: Meduza
content:
Kremlin sources tell Bloomberg that Putin is preparing to escalate the war in Ukraine. A growing number of Russian officials believe that could eventually mean a tactical nuclear weapon.
Russia is preparing to escalate its strikes on Ukraine after concluding that peace talks have hit a dead end, sources close to the Kremlin told Bloomberg.
Here’s what the sources said:
- Russia is weighing stepped-up conventional ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv, including the city center, and on infrastructure in other Ukrainian cities.
- Russian President Vladimir Putin will not end the war under pressure from economic sanctions or Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and logistics networks.
- Moscow increasingly views Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO member states because alliance members supply Kyiv with weapons and intelligence.
- Every mechanism for peace talks has collapsed, leaving the two warring sides back where they started. The Kremlin believes that it has already made concessions during the war and that each one weakened Russia’s position. In the absence of diplomacy, Moscow sees few ways to achieve its military goals other than further escalation.
- The intensifying Ukrainian strikes have led a growing number of Russian officials to believe that Putin could eventually take the extreme step of using tactical nuclear weapons in Ukraine.
Bloomberg said there are no signs that Russia is preparing to use tactical nuclear weapons in Ukraine. In the past, Russia has repeatedly made nuclear threats in an effort to intimidate Ukraine’s Western allies.
Alexander Gabuev, director of the Berlin-based Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, told Bloomberg the risk of Moscow using tactical nuclear weapons remains extremely low.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not respond to a request for comment.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.
Cover photo: Gleb Garanich / Reuters / Scanpix / LETA
summary: According to Kremlin sources cited by Bloomberg, Russian President Vladimir Putin is preparing to escalate the war in Ukraine following the breakdown of all peace talks. The potential escalation could involve stepped-up conventional missile strikes on Kyiv and infrastructure, with a growing number of officials believing it could eventually lead to tactical nuclear weapons. However, Bloomberg noted that there are currently no signs of preparations for nuclear use, and experts view the risk as extremely low.
key_points: Russia is reportedly preparing to escalate strikes on Ukraine after concluding that peace talks have failed.
Moscow is weighing increased conventional ballistic missile strikes against Kyiv and infrastructure in other cities.
The Kremlin increasingly views Ukrainian attacks as actions by NATO due to Western weapon and intelligence supplies.
A growing number of Russian officials believe Putin could eventually use tactical nuclear weapons.
Bloomberg and experts emphasize that there are no signs of nuclear preparations and the risk remains extremely low.

title: Army chief was ousted days after being told to drop Kid Rock investigation: report
author: Alex Woodward
content:
Days before Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted him earlier this year, the Army’s top general was reportedly told by the official who is now trying to replace him to drop an investigation into the military’s unauthorized helicopter flyby at Kid Rock’s property.
Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George was abruptly forced to retire less than two months into the U.S. war in Iran, without explanation, in April. The Pentagon announced his departure in a brief statement on social media, saying “we wish him well in his retirement.”
Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army’s second-highest ranking officer who is now the acting Army chief of staff, reportedly told George that Hegseth did not want the investigation to move forward, according to The Washington Post, citing people familiar with the discussions.
George was then forced to step down, according to the newspaper, clearing a path for Hegseth to nominate LaNeve, the secretary’s top aide, to lead the largest branch of the U.S. armed forces amid growing concerns about Hegseth’s leadership.
The Donald Trump-aligned country-rock performer revealed the flyby in videos posted on social media — taken during nationwide “No Kings” demonstration against the Trump administration — showing two helicopters near his Tennessee mansion as he saluted and cheered. The incident drew fierce outrage over military “joyrides” for what appeared to be a politically fueled statement in support of Trump’s MAGA coalition.
![Apache helicopters performed a flyby at Kid Rock’s Nashville property in March, prompting the pilots’ suspensions and a Pentagon investigation. Secretary Pete Hegseth reversed the decisions and then allegedly forced the Army chief into retirement](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/03/30/13/49/US-Army-helicopter-does-a-fly-by-for-Trumps-pal-Kid-Rock.png)
The flight involved two Apache helicopters from the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade stationed at Fort Campbell.
On March 31, three days after the incident, the Army announced the pilots were suspended and launched an investigation. That same day, Hegseth reversed the decision.
“Thank you Kid Rock,” Hegseth wrote on X at the time. “[U.S. Army] pilots suspension LIFTED. No punishment. No investigation. Carry on, patriots.”
A spokesperson for the 101st Airborne Division said in a statement at the time that the helicopters were not tied to “No Kings” protests in Nashville, which drew thousands of participants.
Kid Rock later told the Associated Press that he spoke to the pilots, saying, “I think they know this is a pretty friendly spot.”
“I’ve talked to some of these pilots,” he added. “I’ve told them, ‘You guys see me waving when you come by the house?’ I’m like, ‘You guys are always welcome to cruise by my house, any time.’”
He also praised the pilots on social media while taking a swipe at California Governor Gavin Newsom. “This is a level of respect that s*** for brains Governor of California will never know,” Kid Rock wrote. “God Bless America and all those who have made the ultimate sacrifice to defend her.”
Trump told reporters at the White House on March 31 that he didn’t see the videos.
“I'm sure they had a good time,” the president said. “Well, they probably shouldn’t have been doing it. You’re not supposed to be playing games, right? But I’d take a look at it. They like Kid Rock? I like Kid Rock. Maybe they were trying to defend him.”
![Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George was reportedly forced into retirement after refusing to drop an investigation into the flyby](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/04/23/09/2264407224.jpg)
George was expected to serve as the Army’s chief of staff through 2027 to finish a typical four-year assignment in the role.
Hegseth instead asked him to retire, effective immediately, days after the helicopter incident. A few weeks later, Hegseth and Kid Rock flew in Apache helicopters from Fort Belvoir in Virginia.
“Kid Rock is a patriot and huge supporter of our troops,” Hegseth wrote in a post on social media alongside photos of himself and the musician at the base.
George declined to comment to The Washington Post, and Pentagon officials did not respond to questions about LaNeve, whose nomination for Army chief of staff is still tied up in Congress.
If the Senate will not vote to confirm LaNeve on a permanent basis, Hegseth can try to keep him on as acting chief of staff indefinitely.
In a statement to The Post, the secretary described LaNeve as “precisely the kind of leader the U.S. Army needs right now” who is “not interested in playing politics in Washington.”
“He is a back-to-basics, no politics, no-nonsense General — exactly what President Trump expects,” Hegseth said, according to The Post. “The critics coming after him are the same out-of-touch so-called insiders who’ve spent years undermining our military with woke policies and endless wars. They hold deep grudges against any commander willing to put America and our troops first, but their days of influence are over.”
summary: Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George was abruptly forced into retirement in April after being told to drop an investigation into an unauthorized military helicopter flyby at Kid Rock's Tennessee property. Gen. Christopher LaNeve reportedly delivered the message that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted the probe halted, clearing the way for LaNeve to be nominated as acting Army chief. Hegseth had previously reversed the suspension of the pilots involved in the March flyby and later flew in an Apache helicopter with Kid Rock.
key_points: Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George was abruptly forced to retire in April following a dispute over an investigation.
Gen. Christopher LaNeve reportedly told George that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted the probe into an unauthorized helicopter flyby at Kid Rock's property dropped.
Hegseth had previously intervened to lift the suspensions of the pilots involved in the March flyby and praised Kid Rock.
Following George's departure, Hegseth nominated LaNeve, his top aide, to serve as the acting Army chief of staff.

title: Nepal-Tibet flash floods: British girl, 13, among hundreds missing in Rasuwa
author: Lily Shanagher; Alexandra Snow; Memphis Barker; Samuel Montgomery; Samaan Lateef
content:
Xi Jinping ordered authorities to step up rescue efforts, state news agency Xinhua reported.
The Chinese president also called for residents at risk to be evacuated from any area on the Chinese side.
Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV, with major casualties reported.
Narendra Modi also spoke with Nepal’s prime minister Balendra Shah and offered India’s help.
“India is prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance. Our teams are closely coordinating on rescue and relief efforts,” he said on social media.
In a joint statement, Australia, Britain, the European Union, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland expressed solidarity with the affected people in Nepal, adding: “We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.”
The EU also announced it had activated its satellite surveillance system to help recovery efforts after the floods in Nepal, and was ready to provide more help.
“Copernicus has been activated to help map the affected areas in Nepal and support the response on the ground,” Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission chief, wrote online.
“We stand ready to mobilise further European assistance.”
summary: Severe flash floods along the Nepal-Tibet border have left hundreds missing, including a 13-year-old British girl in Rasuwa, prompting large-scale search and rescue operations in Tibet's Gyirong area. Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered intensified rescue efforts and evacuations, while international leaders and nations—including India, Britain, Australia, and the EU—offered humanitarian assistance and solidarity. The EU specifically activated its Copernicus satellite surveillance system to map affected regions and support ongoing recovery efforts.
key_points: A 13-year-old British girl is among hundreds missing following flash floods in Rasuwa, Nepal.
Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered intensified rescue operations and evacuations on the Chinese side of the border in Gyirong.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi offered humanitarian assistance and coordinated rescue efforts with Nepal.
Several nations and international bodies, including Britain, Australia, and the EU, expressed solidarity and issued safety advisories.
The European Union activated its Copernicus satellite system to map affected areas and assist recovery.

title: Irish couple found dead in hot tub at Spanish holiday villa
author: James C Reynolds
content:
An Irish couple were found dead in a hot tub by their teenage children at a holiday rental property in Spain on Tuesday, police said.
The bodies of a man, aged 50, and a woman, aged 45, were found at the upscale property in Cullera, on the Valencian coast, on Monday afternoon, according to the Civil Guard.
A spokesperson told The Independent that their children, aged 14 and 15, found their parents dead and that a police investigation is now under way.
![Cullera is a town of around 25,000 people situated some 25 miles south of Valencia.](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/9/15/iStock-1471678755-dde49137.jpeg)
An official previously told the Irish Independent that a homicide team was investigating the case.
“That doesn’t mean that it is a homicide situation because the cause of death is not clear yet,” they qualified. “We have to make sure to preserve all proof and evidence at this stage and to carry on the investigation in case it was not an accident.”
The Civil Guard spokesperson said initial reports now indicate that foul play was not the cause of death.
Officers took samples of cloudy water from the hot tub for analysis, while the bodies were taken to the Institute of Legal Medicine in Valencia city for examination, according to The Times.
They were removed from the scene just before midnight on Tuesday, The Sun reported.
A source close to the investigation told the Irish Independent: “It’s normal a water sample was taken from the jacuzzi the couple were found in. The analysis could help investigators for example in finding out whether it contains DNA belonging to a third person.”
The family are understood to have been staying at the residential development on holiday. Relatives were reportedly making arrangements to travel out to care for the children, who were said to have been receiving psychological support.
Cullera is a town of around 25,000 people situated some 25 miles south of Valencia.
summary: An Irish couple in their forties and fifties were found dead in a hot tub by their teenage children at a holiday rental property in Cullera, Spain. Police and a homicide team opened an investigation to determine the cause of death, though initial reports indicate foul play was not involved. Water samples from the jacuzzi and the bodies were taken for analysis, while the children received psychological support.
key_points: An Irish man and woman were found dead in a hot tub at a Spanish holiday villa.
The bodies were discovered by the couple's 14- and 15-year-old children.
Initial police reports indicate that foul play was not the cause of death.
Investigators took water samples from the hot tub and sent the bodies for examination.
Relatives were making arrangements for the children, who received psychological support.

title: Flash flood on Nepal-Tibet border kills at least 95, with hundreds of foreign tourists missing
author: Live Reporting Edited by Angus Thompson; Craig Hoyle; With Phanindra Dahal; Laura Bicker
content:
By Charlotte Green
Verified videos of the flash floods show two different bridges over the Trishuli river breaking in half after being struck by debris from other bridges swept away further upstream.
BBC Verify has identified one clip as showing Ghatbesi bridge, which is more than 17 miles (27km) to the west and downriver of the videos from Trishuli town we reported on earlier.
The debris, which includes sections of another bridge, smashes into Ghatbesi bridge, splitting it in two before the flood carries it downstream.
![Screenshot of a video showing debris from a bridge smashing another bridge in two](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/8/26/dd42788b-eeee-42ef-9035-faaf43f88e36.png.webp) Image source, X
The second video shows the Dhadingbesi bridge, about 4 miles (6km) further to the west downstream of Ghatbesi, also being struck by violent floodwaters carrying the remains of a bridge.
![Screenshot of a video showing debris from a bridge smashing another bridge in two](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/640/cpsprodpb/vivo/live/images/2026/8/26/206fa4f8-3263-4d38-bf9c-42ecad13d5f2.png.webp) Image source, X
summary: Verified videos of a flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border capture the destruction of two bridges along the Trishuli river. Debris from upstream bridges swept away the Ghatbesi bridge and subsequently struck the Dhadingbesi bridge further downstream, splitting both in half.
key_points: Flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border caused widespread bridge destruction.
BBC Verify identified footage showing the Ghatbesi bridge breaking in half after being struck by upstream debris.
A second video showed the Dhadingbesi bridge, located further west and downriver, being hit by the violent floodwaters and bridge remains.

title: At least 22 killed, hundreds missing after Nepal flash flood
author: AFP; AP; Reuters
content:
![Residents watch a torrent of muddy water surge through a river.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a8ea4623cc7-1787733090.jpg?resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
At least 22 people have been killed and hundreds are missing after a huge flash flood swept away villages in Nepal, damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.
Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries including the United Kingdom, the United States, India and Malaysia were reported missing as a result of the flash flood on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4What caused Nepal’s devastating flood damage and how was it contained?
- list 2 of 4After the floods of 2025, can we keep 2026 above water?
- list 3 of 4Landslide hits bus in northern India, killing 15, as rescue continues
- list 4 of 4Rescuers search for survivors amid risk of fresh floods in Afghanistan
The waters were too high for helicopters to land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, officials said.
“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” district administrator Narendra Pariyar told the Reuters news agency. “But I cannot say for sure now.”
Pariyar urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi River in the area to seek higher ground, pointing to reports that nearby villages and infrastructure project sites were washed away.
Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with people missing in the neighbouring county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a land crossing between China and Nepal, the Xinhua official news agency said.
The mudslide hit China’s Gyirong port, cutting off roads, communications and power in the Shigatse region, Xinhua added, without giving details.
President Xi Jinping urged “all-out” efforts to search for the missing, and called for strengthening monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.
Prayash Adhikari, a climate justice activist in Nepal, said the “devastating” flood has wiped out “whole villages”.
“Hundreds of people are missing,” Adhikari told Al Jazeera from Kathmandu, stating it wiped out buildings, schools, bridges and highways.
Electricity supply disrupted
Videos shared by Nepal Police and others on social media showed torrents of muddy water crashing through mountain valleys.
Many people were caught off guard when the flash flood hit, as there was no heavy rainfall, said Kosh Raj Koirala, an editor of Republica Daily, an English newspaper in Nepal’s capital.
“[People] were at home … several houses have been washed away, swept away by the river,” Koirala told Al Jazeera.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah convened an emergency meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority to take stock of the situation.
“Work has started to take necessary steps in coordination with the medical team, scouts, and Red Cross,” Shah said in a social media post.
![Damaged property and flooded roads following a flash flood in Galchhi in the Dhading district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Picture taken with a mobile phone. REUTERS/Stringer](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/reuters_6a8ea3d3-1787732947.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
The Nepal Army said it had deployed helicopters and disaster response personnel to the affected area.
“The work of collecting details of the damage is under way,” it said in a statement.
The Nepal Electricity Authority said about 430 megawatts of production capacity, including from hydropower and solar facilities, have been damaged.
“The disaster has damaged the production, transmission and distribution facilities of the Authority … resulting in disruption of electricity supply,” it said.
Eight South Koreans working on a hydropower plant were missing, and 10 others were stranded, South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
The workers were employed by two companies, Korea Energy and Doosan Enerbility Co, the ministry said, adding that Nepal has deployed a rescue team to search the affected area.
South Korea, meanwhile, has established a task force led by the foreign minister and plans to send a joint rapid-response team comprising government officials and fire and police authorities to Nepal as soon as possible.
Avalanche could have triggered flood
The exact cause of the flash flood was not immediately clear. Climate experts at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development in Nepal say an avalanche from a glacier likely triggered the flooding.
The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, witnessed maximum flooding on Wednesday, they said.
“The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.
Adhikari, the climate activist, told Al Jazeera that early warning systems are crucial to protect communities.
“This can’t be completely turned around because we are on the verge of climate catastrophe, but still we can protect our communities,” he said.
The Bhote Koshi River originates in Tibet and empties into Nepal’s Trishuli River, which eventually flows into India as the Gandak River.
A flood last year in the Bhote Koshi River killed nine people, with 24 missing, and washed away the “Friendship Bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting transport and trade for several months. That flood was triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.
Monsoon rains from June to September regularly trigger deadly floods and landslides across South Asia.
Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in the region.
![Rescue personnel use an excavator to carry a person affected by flash floods at Devghat in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026.](https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/afp_6a8edbe4bedc-1787747300.jpg?w=770&resize=770%2C513&quality=80)
summary: At least 22 people were killed and hundreds are missing after a massive flash flood swept through villages, roads, and power projects in Nepal near Tibet. High waters initially prevented rescue helicopters from landing in the affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in Rasuwa district. Climate experts stated that an ice rock avalanche from a glacier likely triggered the sudden flooding.
key_points: At least 22 fatalities and hundreds of missing individuals, including 384 tourists, were reported following the flash flood.
The disaster damaged roads, bridges, buildings, and approximately 430 megawatts of electricity production capacity.
Across the border in Tibet, a mudslide hit China's Gyirong port, causing major casualties and cutting off roads and communications.
Climate experts indicated an ice rock avalanche from a glacier likely triggered the sudden surge on the Lhende Khola River.
The Nepal Army deployed helicopters and disaster response personnel while Prime Minister Balendra Shah convened an emergency meeting.

title: Wiped out: US faces surging toilet paper prices amid trade war with Canada
author: Lauren Aratani
content:
Using the bathroom or having a cry is about to become more expensive for North Americans as the US and Canada enter a full-fledged trade war that threatens to flush away decades of peaceful trading between the two nations.
After trade negotiations broke down between the two countries last weekend, Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, vowed to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar” and unveiled a list of nearly 900 American goods that will face 25% to 50% tariffs starting on 8 September.
Paper products are among the hardest-hit sectors, with Canada threatening to put tariffs of between 25% and 50% on “toilet paper or face tissue stock” from 8 September in retaliation for a 50% hike from Washington DC.
Though American toilet paper and tissues are often made domestically, they heavily rely on lumber-rich Canada for raw materials. Procter & Gamble, the owner of Charmin toilet paper, said last year that it would have to increase prices amid tariffs that were in place at the time.
The US imported $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024, according to the World Bank, making it by far the largest exporter of the product to the US. Retailers including Costco source much of their paper products from the country.
The US accounts for more than 20% of global tissue consumption despite having only 4% of the world’s population. The average American uses 141 rolls of toilet paper per year, making them No 1 for No 2s globally, just ahead of Germans, each using an average of 134 rolls annually.
It’s not just paper products that could rise in price. The trade war highlights the deep economic ties shared between the two countries as consumers continue to worry about inflation on both sides of the border.
US tariffs are specifically affecting Canadian liquor, including popular whiskey brands Crown Royal and Canadian Club, which are currently under a 50% tariff.
While Canada has not introduced a tariff on American liquor, most Canadian provinces have introduced their own bans on American alcohol, in retaliation for earlier tariffs on Canadian products. Donald Trump used these province-wide bans on American alcohol as part of his legal justification for his new tariffs against Canada.
Carney has asked province leaders to consider putting American liquor back on the shelves, though as the Nova Scotia premier Tim Houston told CBC News: “Whether Nova Scotians or Canadians will actually buy it when it’s back on the shelves, that’s a whole other discussion.”
after newsletter promotion
Trump also said that his new tariffs are in retaliation for Canadian levies against the American dairy industry. He introduced a 50% tariff on nearly all Canadian dairy products, with the exception of Canadian cheese.
In response, Canada has a 50% tariff on American dairy products, along with a 25% tariff on American cheese.
Canada also took a swing at the US fishing industry, with a 25% tariff on American fish and seafood, including frozen lobster. The move prompted Republican senator Susan Collins, facing a tough re-election battle in lobster-capital Maine, to call Trump’s latest move “a mistake”.
A 25% tariff on Canadian cars and auto parts is set to affect the American auto industry, which relies heavily on Canadian parts for manufacturing. Trump has threatened to double the tariff to 50% if a deal isn’t made by 1 January 2027.
With negotiations down the drain, it’s unclear if or when the tariffs will be lifted. But the Trump administration is adamant that “there’s no possible way” the trade dispute with Canada will affect US consumers, according to Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative.
“The fundamentals are good,” he said. “I don’t think this is going to affect anything.”
summary: A trade war between the US and Canada is causing surging prices for consumer goods, particularly paper products like toilet paper and tissues which rely on Canadian raw materials. Following the breakdown of trade negotiations, both nations have implemented mutual tariffs ranging from 25% to 50% on various goods including dairy, alcohol, seafood, and auto parts. While the Trump administration claims the dispute will not affect US consumers, businesses and officials on both sides warn of rising inflation and economic fallout.
key_points: Canada announced 25% to 50% tariffs on nearly 900 American goods starting September 8 in response to US tariffs.
American paper products, including toilet paper and tissues, face steep price hikes because they rely heavily on Canadian raw lumber materials.
The US is the world's largest consumer of tissue products, importing $328m worth of toilet paper from Canada in 2024.
Both countries have exchanged retaliatory tariffs impacting key industries such as dairy, seafood, liquor, and auto manufacturing.

title: At least 14 newborn babies die in fire at Pakistan hospital’s maternity ward
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen; Shah Meer Baloch
content:
At least 14 newborn babies have died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward at one of Pakistan’s most prominent state hospitals.
The blaze began in the early hours of Wednesday and engulfed the ward at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences, the biggest state hospital in Islamabad.
A statement by the hospital administration confirmed that 14 newborn babies in the intensive care unit (ICU) had died in the fire.
Dr Aneeza Jalil, a hospital spokesperson, told the Dawn newspaper that 15 babies were on the ward at the time and that “one baby was saved by a doctor”. Women who had just given birth were forced to run down several flights of stairs and climb out of windows and down ladders to evacuate.
The health minister, Mustafa Kamal, said many of the babies had been in incubators or on oxygen, and that the oxygen canisters had made the fire worse.
Kamal suggested the blaze had been caused by an air conditioner, but investigators were still at the scene and authorities have not confirmed the cause. Repair works and construction were ongoing at the hospital.
![Two police officers looking from two broken windows](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d29992a15f54e81ed13922d26872ebb1e507012c/583_0_5831_4665/master/5831.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Among the witnesses was Sardar Atti ur Rehman, 38, whose wife had given birth to a girl at the hospital the previous day. He had been sleeping at the hospital and rushed into the maternity ward as the fire was spreading, desperately looking for his wife and child.
He described scenes of panic as thick smoke filled the ward. “I could not see my family including my newborn baby in the room but kept searching,” he said. “My heart was heavy.”
He said he saw a woman laid out on a stretcher and helped to drag her out of the ward, but that other women refused to leave as they cried out for their babies.
“I saw a mother who was crying and screaming for her child who was admitted inside the ICU,” he said. “I tried to enter the ICU but failed as the smoke was too thick. I could not see anything and I was facing issues to breathe. I begged her that you need to save yourself and we will look for the child later.”
Rehman said there had been few staff on the ward at the time of the fire and that the families were left to fend for themselves.
Sohail Ashraf, the Islamabad chief commissioner, said the emergency call was made just before 7am, with rescue and police teams quickly reaching the scene.
![A group of women in hijabs outside the hospital](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e7802e0244cdca3bfaa2c342d5f66f1b549b1a01/40_0_1201_960/master/1201.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
“The fire was immediately brought under control and the children were immediately shifted to the intensive care unit,” said the hospital administration’s statement.
Alamzaib Khan, 26, was also among those who tried to run into the ward as it burned. His wife had given birth to a baby girl two days ago and both mother and baby were still in the hospital as she recovered from a C-section.
“I was sleeping on the pavement when I heard people screaming and wailing,” he said. “I ran towards the ICU and children’s ward and I saw my wife while climbing down a ladder.”
After checking on his wife, he tried to help with the rescue efforts of others. “The moment I approached the children’s ward, I couldn’t see anything because the smoke was so thick. I tried to go inside but it was not possible.”
He said he found out later that his daughter had been moved from the ward and had survived.
“People were crying, screaming and asking for help. Women from the operation room had to run for their lives,” he said. “Women were in pain themselves but crying and begging everyone to help them to rescue their children. It’s hard to describe this terrible moment.”
The prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, directed authorities to conduct an immediate investigation into the incident, which was one of the deadliest hospital fires in years.
“Such a situation involving children is irreparable,” said Sharif. “Those responsible should be identified, and the strictest action should be taken.”
Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, expressed condolences to the families of the newborn babies. In a statement, he said that the loss of lives was “heartbreaking”.
Fires in large buildings such as factories and shopping malls are frequent in Pakistan, often due to poor safety laws and lax enforcement of building codes.
summary: At least 14 newborn babies died in a fire that broke out in the maternity ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad. The early morning blaze quickly filled the intensive care unit with thick smoke, while oxygen canisters reportedly worsened the flames. Officials stated that 15 babies were in the ward, with only one being saved by a doctor. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation to identify those responsible.
key_points: A fire in the maternity ward of Islamabad's Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences resulted in the deaths of 14 newborn babies.
Out of 15 infants in the ward during the blaze, only one was successfully rescued by a doctor.
The health minister noted that oxygen canisters worsened the fire, and a malfunction involving an air conditioner is suspected as the cause.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered an immediate investigation into the deadly incident.
New mothers and family members described scenes of panic, thick smoke, and chaotic evacuation efforts.

title: Ukraine war live: Kyiv agreed not to strike Russia amid CIA chief’s mysterious visit
author: Maira Butt; James Reynolds; Arpan Rai
content:
Ukraine heeded a special request from the Donald Trump administration not to attack major Russian cities during a visit by CIA director John Ratcliffe.
The US contacted Kyiv last week to request that it not strike Moscow, St Petersburg and a stretch of northern Russia while a plane carrying the senior US official was flying in and out of the Russian capital, sources told Reuters.
The request covered Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday and was only revealed hours after Ratcliffe left Russia late on Tuesday.
Subsequently, a large US military aircraft was confirmed to have travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday, flight tracking data confirmed.
The purpose of Ratcliffe’s visit and the nature of his meetings in Russia were not immediately clear. It was the first known trip to Moscow by a US spy chief since his predecessor, William Burns, held talks with Vladimir Putin in November 2021.
Ukraine resumed strikes on Russia early on Wednesday after Ratcliffe's departure, with Russia saying it downed at least 426 drones overnight.
Energy secretary says 'I can't control wars' in defending Ofgem 4% price cap rise
CIA director met with Russian intelligence during Moscow visit - Kremlin
CIA Director John Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during his visit to Moscow on Tuesday but did not meet President Vladimir Putin, the Kremlin said on Wednesday.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Putin had been briefed on the outcome of Ratcliffe's talks, but declined to provide further details.
Peskov said it was also too early to say whether such contacts between the two countries' intelligence agencies could help pull U.S.-Russia relations out of what he described as a "deep crisis".
Russia summons Romania's charge d'affaires
Russia's Foreign Ministry has summoned Romania's charge d'affaires in Moscow, the Interfax news agency reported on Wednesday.
It did not give a reason for the summons.
Russia and Ukraine exchange 10 POWs
Russia and Ukraine have each exchanged 10 prisoners of war in the latest such trade, according to Interfax.
In pictures: Zelensky meets with former US boxer Terence Crawford
![Zelensky shakes hands with former American professional boxer Terence Crawford](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/08/2026-08-25T203538Z_239240491_RC2W5NA0HSCQ_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-CRAWFORD.JPG)
![Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky holds a puppy of American pit bull terrier named Freya, given to him by former American professional boxer Terence Crawford after their meeting on Tuesday](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/08/2026-08-25T203538Z_108256159_RC2W5NANWRI4_RTRMADP_3_UKRAINE-CRISIS-CRAWFORD.JPG)
Repairs at Russia's Novorossiysk grain terminal may take up to four months, company says
It could take up to four months to restore damaged facilities at NKHP, one of the largest grain terminals at Russia's port of Novorossiysk, where operations have been halted since August, the company said on Wednesday in its financial report.
Local officials said earlier in August that a Ukrainian drone and missile strike on the port damaged two major grain export terminals and hit the last big Russian naval base on the Black Sea.
Burnham warned Russia plotting retaliation against Britain over support for Ukraine - report
Andy Burnham was reportedly warned that Russia is plotting retaliation against Britain for its continued support for Ukraine.
Security experts were said to have told the prime minister to be ready for a ‘direct response’, according to the Daily Mail.
Mr Burnham travelled to Kyiv on Monday for his first overseas trip since taking office last month and said London and Paris would provide long-range missile technology to Ukraine.
A unnamed senior security source told the Mail: “An attack on the UK’s defence and security infrastructure is inevitable, based on our high profile support for Ukraine.
“Ourselves and the French are front and centre, and Burnham's visit to Kyiv and his forthright stance will have been noticed at the Kremlin,” they assessed.
“There had been some optimism in Moscow that he would be softer than Starmer on Ukraine. That was not the case.”
![Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, right, welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham to Kyiv on Monday (Henry Nicholls/PA)](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/25/12/d1b240a04d24db3e718320a8e8a1ea25Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg3NzQyMDEz-2.85651414.jpg)
Release of Marine veteran from Russian custody turns focus to other detainees with health concerns
Robert Gilman’s release from Russian custody this month heralded a long-awaited homecoming for the Marine veteran after more than four years behind bars.
But as Harold Jezler followed the media coverage from the United States, he couldn’t help but notice Gilman’s gaunt and sickly appearance and think of the implications for his wife, Olga, who has been detained in Russia since 2022 and faces her own health problems.
“You just look at the pictures and the guy is not in good shape. It’s concerning for me and for all the families, I would imagine," Jezler said in an interview with The Associated Press. "Is this what it takes for the government to really make a move and prioritize this — that the person is basically in dire straits? It was a very bittersweet thing to see that."
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/26/05/American_Detainees_Russia_8563_.jpg?width=1200&height=800&crop=1200:800)
Russia downs 426 drones overnight, says Russian media citing defence ministry
Russia downed 426 drones overnight, Russian news agencies quoted the defence ministry as saying. The figure includes Russia-controlled parts of Ukraine.
Russia says it struck five vessels in Ukraine's Black Sea ports
The Russian defence ministry said that its forces had struck three cargo vessels carrying supplies for the Ukrainian military and a tanker at the Black Sea port of Pivdennyi yesterday.
The ministry also said it had hit another cargo vessel in the nearby port of Odesa, as well as port infrastructure in Pivdennyi and Odesa and fuel storage facilities at the port of Chornomorsk.
summary: Ukraine temporarily halted strikes on major Russian cities following a special request from the U.S. administration during a visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials but did not meet President Vladimir Putin. Ukraine resumed its drone attacks shortly after his departure.
key_points: Ukraine agreed not to target major Russian cities during CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow.
Ratcliffe met with Russian intelligence officials, though Vladimir Putin did not attend the meeting.
Ukraine resumed drone strikes against Russia immediately following Ratcliffe's departure.
Russia and Ukraine exchanged 10 prisoners of war each.

title: Wednesday briefing: How Canada has turned a trade dispute into a defence of its sovereignty
author: Libby Brooks
content:
Good morning. When the Guardian asked Canadian readers whether they planned to boycott US products after dramatic escalations in the ongoing DC/Ottawa trade war, we received more than 2,000 responses within 12 hours.
This inundation is perhaps evidence of the existential crisis many Canadians feel they now face, something often lost in the granular reporting of trade negotiations: this is about so much more than the price of lumber.
Assailed by a US president who has repeatedly expressed a desire to consume Canada into a supersized 51st state, the country has felt perpetually on the brink of war – albeit an economic one – since Donald Trump’s early second-term tariff salvo in February 2025. This culminated in Canada’s finance minister announcing tit-for-tat tariffs on key American industries yesterday, further incensing the US president.
Canadian PM Mark Carney has emerged as a leader whose refusal to be dominated by Trump is underpinned by an ambition to reorder global politics. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to the Guardian’s Canada correspondent Leyland Cecco about trade narratives, Carney’s grand plan and the price of fruit in his local grocery store. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories
- 
  US news | Dolly Parton, one of the greatest singer-songwriters in country music who was also much cherished for her philanthropy, has died aged 80.
- 
  UK news | UK citizens will be told to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies as part of a new government campaign to improve the nation’s resilience.
- 
  UK politics | Andy Burnham will face an immediate test of his backing for electoral reform in his first week in parliament as prime minister, with almost 100 Labour MPs supporting a bid for a new national commission.
- 
  Ukraine | A man from South Yorkshire is believed to be the first British citizen to die fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
- 
  Climate crisis | The carbon emissions from just two planned datacentres in England will exceed all of the fossil fuel company ExxonMobil’s UK emissions, analysis has revealed.
In depth: ‘If we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu’
![Canadian prime minister Mark Carney speaks about the trade dispute with the United States at the Davie shipyard in Levis, Quebec, Canada on 24 August 2026.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/77ac28df776655b410c7bcdafebde8a7c00ee380/255_0_4490_3592/master/4490.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The United States and Canada have enjoyed one of the strongest bilateral relationships in recent history. They share the longest unprotected border in the world, along with deep trading, security and cultural ties.
But the second Trump presidency has brought about a fundamental breach in the shared values and understanding that once united the two nations. Trump has repeatedly threatened to annex Canada, as he yearns to access its critical minerals.
Carney, a former Governor of the Bank of England, was sworn in as prime minister last year in the midst of Trump’s tariff wars, having never held elected public office before. He has since become the first western leader to openly acknowledge the hazard Trump poses to the global order. In a high-profile January speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, he urged “middle powers” like Canada to “act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu.”
Tariffs appear to have become a proxy for this political rupture. The ongoing US/Canada trade war began in February 2025, when Trump then (briefly) imposed tariffs of 25% on almost all imports from Canada and Mexico. Canada retaliated in kind, and the bitter dispute had just been rumbling on.
Against this backdrop, Leyland tells me, reporters like him are “trying to figure out the magnitude of what’s happened.”
What’s the latest?
Last Tuesday, in a late night Truth Social post (is there any other kind?) Trump declared a “DEAL” with Canada was in its final stages.
Trump delayed for three days the swingeing import taxes he was threatening to impose, which would have affected everything from anoraks to Christmas ornaments. The White House said in July that these 50% tariffs were in retaliation for “discriminatory treatment” by Canada. Still with me?
On Friday, Canadian officials agreed a deal was still close, yet 24 hours later the whole thing fell apart. Canada walked out of negotiations hours before the 50% tariffs on roughly $20bn (£14.6bn) of Canadian goods kicked in on Saturday, with Carney accusing the US of using “economic integration as a weapon”.
Yesterday, Canada pledged to roll out “dollar-for-dollar” retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of US goods next month, prompting Trump to denounce the nation as “difficult and unreasonable”. Precisely how this all unravelled depends on whose narrative you follow.
Carney’s position was that the US was breaching a red line on French language protection. Currently, Canadian rules require companies operating in Quebec, its predominantly Francophone province, to provide French-language goods and services to help protect its cultural identity. These stipulations have frustrated US negotiators.
There’s also a counter narrative, that Canada’s negotiators were conceding so much – for example, accepting tariffs on the auto sector, steel and aluminium – that a number of senior Canadian politicians had urged Carney to harden his resolve.
Meanwhile, US officials accused Canada of collapsing the deal by seeking additional last minute concessions.
In the concurrent war of communications, Carney emerges the winner, says Leyland, “because he can defend the decision to walk way to Canadians”, while the US is hampered both by Trump’s ego and top officials pushing their own agendas. 
How Carney won this round
Polling over the weekend found strong majority support for Carney’s stance in every Canadian province, and a mood of steadfast defiance can be read across Canada’s media. “The coming period will be hard and the damage may be awful but no one should ignore what is at stake. A free Canada is worth the sacrifice,” declared an editorial in the Globe and Mail.
“What we see now is near uniform support for the prime minister ,” says Leyland, “and immense feelings of national unity”. This even extends to successionist Quebec, where support for independence from the rest of Canada is at its lowest level in decades.
Carney – who has consolidated support for his previously ailing Liberals – is enjoying “a key political win” Leyland says, defending totemic language rights that are seen as integral to Canada’s cultural fabric.
But his refusal to bow to US demands is part of a broader strategy. “What we’re seeing right now is the logical extension of that [Davos] speech, which was a warning and also laying the groundwork for how Canada would conduct itself”. For now, Carney is strengthening trade ties with China and the EU, to the chagrin of US negotiators.
“The message is that Canada has long enjoyed a very beneficial relationship with the US and that’s over,” says Leyland. “Now we will walk away from the table if there is any erosion of our sovereignty.”
Compare this Canadian unity with the domestic reaction south of the border: with the midterms looming, Trump is reportedly heading for a tariff-shaped clash with Senate Republicans.
As venerable economist Paul Krugman pointed out yesterday: “The US is far more dependent on Canadian goods than most Americans realise.”
The mood in Canada
“There’s an asymmetric aim in this war,” says Leyland, “which is that Canada is fighting for its sovereignty, its national identity.” The US, meanwhile, is just “fighting for cheaper goods”.
This perhaps explains why boycotting US goods has such visceral and consistent support among Canadians. A grassroots boycott has emerged as a consumer-driven response to the tariff war, with supermarket scanning apps like Maple Scan springing up to help users buy Canadian.
Leyland is a parent of two young kids who like to eat berries – now he analyses every package in the grocery aisle to work out where they were grown. “I remember there was a period when US berries were on the steepest discount because they just weren’t selling.”
